review.text: As the daughter of a veterinarian, I have very high expectations when it comes to veterinary care, and I can honestly say that Dr. Dogra and Dr. Sharma have exceeded them.
The level of kindness, competence, and care I experienced here is something I haven't encountered in over a decade of being a pet owner. Hands down the best vet I've ever been to.

Thankfully, I found this clinic, and they saw her the very same day. Dr. Dogra and the team were so kind, compassionate, and reassuring from the moment we walked in. They quickly found an abscessed tooth and treated it right away.
I've brought so many animals to Dr Dogra over the years through my job, and he is hands-down one of the best vets I have ever worked with. We had clients who drove from two hours away to go to him.
I have been in the animal services field for over 35 years and I highly recommend this veterinary practice.
We had never encountered a vet so far in 13 yrs to go in such details with so much passion and honest assessments.

It was so evident just how much Dr. Crippen cared for Jack and my grandmother all these years. Dr. Crippen was prepared with all of his vet records and truly helped this tough time become a smooth transition.

First he evaluated and then safely did a wonderful job of dental cleaning and tooth extractions on Max, who by age was a higher risk patient. It all went fantastic and we are so pleased we chose him for the procedure.
I figured the cost would be something I could not afford but it turned out great and my dog for the first time is happy with no pain.
Also, our pet needed a dental procedure, and honestly the price was way better than other places we called.
The vets are communicative and caring, the front office staff are efficient and knowledgeable and you can get an appointment within at most a couple days.
Every detail was perfect. The doctor even phoned the following day to see if pup was doing well.
Dr. Dogra took incredible care of our cat when he was injured and very ill. We never felt rushed; he always gave us time, attention, and support.
Dr. Dogra was extremely kind, very communicative and took great care of my dog for a dental procedure.
We took our rescue dog to the vet for an emergency scenario and they took care of him like he was their own. I'm forever grateful for their care and services.
Amazing service! Helped me out with an emergency last minute on a Friday so grateful thank you so much!!
My cats get great care from Dr. Dogra here at this clinic! I appreciate how easy it is to schedule and they have great dental care specials and services as well.

I felt my animals were well taken care of and they listened to me!

health.title: Most lumps are nothing. Some aren't.
health.body: The only way to know is to check. A quick needle sample often gives an answer the same visit — and finding out early is what keeps a small problem small.

health.title: Ears that keep flaring up are telling you something
health.body: Repeat ear infections are usually a symptom, not the problem. Allergies are the most common cause underneath. Treating the ear alone means treating it again in two months.

health.title: Limping that comes and goes still counts
health.body: Arthritis rarely arrives all at once. Dogs slow down on stairs; cats stop jumping to the counter. Both are treatable, and earlier is meaningfully better.

health.title: Drinking more than usual is worth a call
health.body: Increased thirst is one of the earliest signs of kidney disease, diabetes, and thyroid problems. It's easy to dismiss and easy to test for.

health.title: The litter box is a health record
health.body: Changes in frequency, volume, or straining are often the first sign of a urinary or kidney problem. If something looks different, tell us — the details matter more than you'd think.

health.title: A straining male cat is an emergency
health.body: A cat going in and out of the box producing little or nothing may have a blocked urethra. That becomes life-threatening within hours. Call immediately — don't wait to see if it passes.

health.title: A cat who stops eating can't wait
health.body: Cats who go without food for a couple of days risk serious liver complications. Skipping one meal happens; skipping several is a reason to be seen.

health.title: Weight loss in a cat is never just age
health.body: It's one of the most reliable early signals we have — thyroid, kidney, diabetes, dental pain. If the scale is dropping, there's usually a reason worth finding.

health.title: Heart murmurs are silent to you
health.body: There are no symptoms you could notice at home. It takes a stethoscope and a quiet minute — which is one of the quieter reasons an annual exam earns its place.

health.title: A coughing dog isn't always a cold
health.body: Cough can come from the airways, the heart, or both. Telling them apart changes the treatment completely, so it's worth having us listen rather than waiting it out.

health.title: Behavior change is medical until proven otherwise
health.body: Hiding, irritability, house-soiling, or new clinginess are how pets report pain and illness. It's rarely spite and rarely just aging.

health.title: A microchip is only as good as its contact info
health.body: Phone numbers change, people move, and the chip can't tell anyone that. Updating your registration takes two minutes and it's what turns a scan into a phone call home. Ask us to check yours.

health.title: Age is not a disease
health.body: Older pets aren't automatically poor anesthesia candidates. What matters is organ function and blood pressure — things we can actually measure before deciding.

health.title: The first sixteen weeks matter most
health.body: Puppy and kitten vaccine series work because of the spacing, not just the shots. Finishing on schedule is what closes the window where they're still vulnerable.

health.title: Feet and nails deserve attention in seniors
health.body: Overgrown nails change how a pet stands, which worsens sore joints. It's a small thing that makes an arthritic dog noticeably more comfortable.

why.rec: We recommend running lab work in house
why.because: Our own lab means results while you're still here for many tests. You leave with answers and a plan instead of waiting days wondering — and for a sick pet, that speed sometimes matters a great deal.

why.rec: We recommend dental x-rays with every cleaning
why.because: Most of a tooth sits below the gumline, where the eye can't reach. Painful roots and hidden resorption look completely normal from above. X-rays are how we avoid leaving the actual problem behind.

why.rec: We recommend an exam every year, even when nothing's wrong
why.because: A year is a long stretch of a pet's life, and most of what we catch early is found on a routine visit by someone who has examined that animal before. Healthy visits are what make sick visits rarer.

why.rec: We recommend a yearly stool sample
why.because: Intestinal parasites are common, often invisible, and several of them can pass to people — especially children. It's an inexpensive test that occasionally changes everything.

why.rec: We recommend heartworm testing before starting prevention
why.because: Giving preventive medication to a dog who already has heartworm can cause a dangerous reaction. The test protects your dog before the prevention can.

why.rec: We recommend baseline bloodwork while your pet is young and well
why.because: Normal ranges are wide, but your individual pet's normal is narrow. Knowing what healthy looks like for them makes an abnormal result years from now far easier to interpret.

why.rec: We recommend a urine sample alongside senior bloodwork
why.because: Urine shows us how the kidneys are actually performing, which blood values alone can miss. Together they catch kidney disease considerably earlier than either does by itself.

why.rec: We recommend blood pressure checks for senior cats
why.because: High blood pressure in cats is common, silent, and can cause sudden blindness. Checking it takes a few quiet minutes and the treatment is straightforward.

why.rec: We recommend pain medication after every surgical procedure
why.because: Pets don't complain, which is exactly why it's easy to under-treat them. Controlled pain also means faster healing and better eating in the days afterward.

why.rec: We recommend coming back for the recheck
why.because: It's the visit that confirms the treatment worked — or catches early that it didn't. Skipping it is how a resolved-looking problem quietly becomes a repeat one.

why.rec: We recommend filling prescriptions where your pet's chart lives
why.because: Every prescription here is checked against your pet's weight, bloodwork, and other medications. That cross-check is the part that isn't printed on the label.

why.rec: We recommend talking to us about food before the internet
why.because: Nutrition advice online is largely marketing, and pet food claims are loosely regulated. A five-minute conversation about your specific pet beats an hour of reading.

why.rec: We recommend a quick weigh-in between visits
why.because: Weight change is the earliest signal we get for a long list of conditions. Stopping by the front desk to use the scale takes a minute and costs nothing.

why.rec: We recommend deciding spay and neuter timing together
why.because: The right age depends on species, breed, and adult size — it isn't one number for every pet. A short conversation gets your pet the timing that fits them.

why.rec: We recommend bringing your pet in before the problem is obvious
why.because: By the time a pet clearly looks unwell, they have usually been compensating for a while. The visits that change outcomes most are the ones that felt slightly premature.

question.q: My pet is old. Is anesthesia safe?
question.a: Age alone isn't the risk — undiagnosed disease is. That's why we check bloodwork and organ function first, then tailor the anesthetic protocol to your individual pet.

question.q: Can I just get the vaccines without an exam?
question.a: Vaccines are medical treatments, so we need to know your pet is well enough to receive them that day. The exam is also where most early problems get found.

question.q: What actually happens in a wellness exam?
question.a: We check weight and body condition, listen to the heart and lungs, look at eyes, ears, skin, and mouth, feel the abdomen and lymph nodes, and assess joints. Then we talk through what we found.

question.q: How do I know if it's an emergency?
question.a: Call us — and if we're closed, our message will point you to the after-hours hospital. Difficulty breathing, a straining male cat, a bloated abdomen, seizures, or uncontrolled bleeding can't wait. When you're unsure, the call costs nothing.

question.q: Why do you need a stool sample?
question.a: Because intestinal parasites usually cause no visible signs until they're well established, and some of them can spread to the people in your household.

question.q: My pet hates coming here. Can we make it easier?
question.a: Yes — and please tell us. Calming medication before the visit, quieter appointment times, and slower handling all help. A frightened pet also gives us a less accurate exam.
We accept CareCredit and Cherry, and we're always willing to talk through what's urgent versus what can wait. Please ask — that conversation is a normal part of care.

question.q: Can I stay with my pet during the exam?
question.a: Usually yes, and many pets do better with you there. For x-rays and certain procedures we'll need to step away for safety reasons, and we'll always explain why.

question.q: Why do you weigh my pet every single visit?
question.a: Because weight trends are one of the most useful pieces of data we have, and because medication doses depend on it. A single pound matters more in a cat than you'd think.

question.q: Should I be brushing my pet's teeth?
question.a: If you can, yes — daily is ideal and even a few times a week helps. Ask us to show you how; most pets accept it better than their owners expect.

question.q: What food should I be feeding?
question.a: It depends on age, weight, and any conditions your pet has. Bring in what you're feeding now and we'll tell you honestly whether it's fine or worth changing.
For many families, yes — especially if an unexpected large bill would be difficult. It's most valuable bought while your pet is young and healthy, before anything becomes pre-existing.

question.q: Will I see the same doctor each time?
question.a: That's the point of a practice this size. You'll see the same small team who know your pet's history, rather than whoever happens to be on shift that day.

question.q: Why does my indoor cat need an exam?
question.a: Cats are remarkably good at hiding illness, and indoor life doesn't prevent kidney disease, thyroid problems, or dental pain. Indoor cats are simply harder to read.

question.q: Will my pet come home the same day after a dental?
question.a: In almost all cases, yes. They go home once they're fully awake and comfortable, with clear instructions and pain medication for the days that follow.

didyou.title: Cats mostly meow at us, not each other
didyou.body: Adult cats rarely meow at other cats. The meow is something they developed largely to communicate with people — your cat is talking to you specifically.

didyou.title: Whiskers are measuring tools
didyou.body: A cat's whiskers are roughly as wide as its body, helping it judge whether a gap is worth squeezing through.

didyou.title: Dogs run a little warm
didyou.body: Normal body temperature for a dog or cat is about 101 to 102.5 degrees — a few degrees warmer than ours. That's why they feel like a hot water bottle on your lap.

didyou.title: Puppies arrive deaf and blind
didyou.body: Eyes and ear canals open at around two weeks. Those first weeks are navigated almost entirely by smell and touch.

didyou.title: Kittens start out blue-eyed
didyou.body: Nearly every kitten is born with blue eyes. Their adult color develops gradually over the following weeks.

didyou.title: Cats walk in their own footprints
didyou.body: A cat's hind paws land almost exactly where the front paws just were. It's called direct registering, and it makes for very quiet movement.

didyou.title: Ears built for listening
didyou.body: A cat's ears are controlled by roughly thirty muscles and can rotate independently to track a sound. Dogs have around eighteen.

didyou.title: Dalmatians are born white
didyou.body: The spots develop over the first weeks of life. Newborn Dalmatian puppies are solid white.

didyou.title: Basenjis don't bark
didyou.body: The breed is known for a yodel-like sound instead — a result of a differently shaped larynx.

didyou.title: Newfoundlands come with webbed feet
didyou.body: Bred for water rescue, they have webbing between the toes and a water-resistant coat.

didyou.title: That funny open-mouthed face has a name
didyou.body: When a cat freezes with its mouth slightly open, it's using the vomeronasal organ on the roof of the mouth to analyze a scent more deeply. It's called the flehmen response.

didyou.title: Cats spend a third of their waking hours grooming
didyou.body: It regulates temperature, spreads natural oils, and calms them down. A cat that suddenly stops grooming is often telling you something.

didyou.title: Hearts that race
didyou.body: A resting cat's heart beats around 140 to 220 times per minute — roughly triple ours. It's one reason a stethoscope exam takes a practiced ear.

didyou.title: Dogs dream too
didyou.body: Brain activity during canine sleep closely resembles the human sleep cycle. Those twitching paws are likely a dream in progress.

didyou.title: Whiskers read the air
didyou.body: A dog's whiskers detect subtle air currents, helping map nearby objects — useful in the dark or in tall grass.

didyou.title: Greyhounds are built for the sprint
didyou.body: They can reach over 40 miles per hour, but only briefly. Most are famously content to spend the rest of the day asleep on the couch.

didyou.title: Cats sleep most of the day
didyou.body: Twelve to sixteen hours is completely normal. Big changes in that pattern, in either direction, are worth mentioning to us.

didyou.title: The head tilt has a purpose
didyou.body: Tilting may help a dog pinpoint where a sound is coming from, and may help them see past their own muzzle to read your face.

didyou.title: About ten percent of a cat's bones are in the tail
didyou.body: It's a long chain of small vertebrae, which is why tail injuries need careful handling.

didyou.title: Retractable by design
didyou.body: A cat's claws sheath when not in use, which keeps them sharp. It's also why cats still need something appropriate to scratch.

didyou.title: Panting is the cooling system
didyou.body: Dogs have very few sweat glands, mostly in the paw pads. Panting does the real work — which is why heat builds dangerously fast in a parked car.

didyou.title: Noses are individual
didyou.body: The pattern of ridges on a pet's nose is unique, much like a fingerprint. Some registries have actually used nose prints as identification.

didyou.title: Cats land on their feet — usually
didyou.body: The righting reflex lets them rotate mid-air, but it isn't magic. Falls from height still cause serious injuries, so screened windows matter.

didyou.title: A dog's hearing reaches well past ours
didyou.body: They pick up frequencies far above the human range, which is why some sounds you can't hear at all will send a dog to the door.

didyou.title: Orange cats are usually male
didyou.body: The gene for orange coloring sits on the X chromosome, which is why roughly three out of four orange tabbies are male.

didyou.title: Tortoiseshell cats are nearly always female
didyou.body: It takes two X chromosomes to produce the pattern. Male torties are rare and usually sterile.

didyou.title: Rough tongues have a job
didyou.body: The backward-facing barbs on a cat's tongue act like a comb, pulling loose fur from the coat — and delivering it straight to the stomach.

didyou.title: Dogs read us closely
didyou.body: They follow human pointing and eye direction better than almost any other species, including our closest primate relatives.

didyou.title: Cats sweat through their paws
didyou.body: Those damp little prints on the exam table aren't nerves alone — paw pads are one of the few places a cat can sweat.

didyou.title: A pet's sense of time is real
didyou.body: Dogs and cats track daily rhythms closely, which is why dinner time gets announced with such confidence.
